utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Pisarevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Savic. Before we resume our examination-in-chief, I would just like to ask you about the fact, related to what you said about the meeting on the 20th, outside the Buducnost factory, that a certain number of persons, citizens of Samac, of all different ethnic groups decided to join the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May counsel please be asked to speak closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Pisarevic, can you find a way of standing closer to the microphone, because these complaints have been repeated so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the procedure like when citizens joined the 4th Detachment? What sort of procedure did they go through?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my speech and after Milos Bogdanovic's speech, those present asked a number of questions regarding this procedure. They asked how they could join the unit or how they could be given work assignments in other places. Milos Bogdanovic, the head of the secretariat for defence, explained the procedure to them, as follows: All those interested in joining the unit, or any other place of work, must come to see him at his office, that is, Milos Bogdanovic. And then he used a document that we refer to as the military booklet, or rather, military ID. He would give them their war assignment and send them to their respective units. Such people, men of military age, conscripts, were the men we received, we from the detachment, and we sent them on to lower-ranking units. There were a number of persons who were not fit for military service and who expressed their desire to have another kind of work assignment. The procedure for those was the same except that in those cases the Ministry of Defence, that is, the secretariat, would adopt a decision to send these people to other work assignments, to the civilian protection or another place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can we wrap this up, please. You couldn't come straight to the army, or rather, to the unit, or receive a work assignment without proper procedure, through the channel of the secretariat for National Defence, headed by Milos Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We broke off yesterday when we talked about the moment when Mr. Radovan Antic told you, the command, what had happened to him. What happened after that? What sort of discussion did you have, members of the command, and where did you go later, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day he told us about what had happened to him, in addition to other things, Simo, myself, and other members of the command, realised that he was in a situation where he couldn't say much. He wasn't able to talk. He simply said: I no longer desire to remain commander under these circumstances. That's what he said. Simo, myself, and other members of the command tried to convince him to stay in that position, in order to keep the team from splitting up. And then the next day, I think it was the 22nd or the 23rd, but I'm not sure, he said: Tomorrow the three of us would go to see the commander, at Pelagicevo. I'll tell him all of this, and I'll tell him that I'm no longer prepared or able to remain the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did you go? Did you go to the command of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, Radovan, Simo, and I went to the command of the 17th Tactical Group in Pelagicevo to see the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Antic tell the commander then? What did he inform him about?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Antic informed the commander in detail about what had happened to him. At first, the commander could not accept the treatment that Antic had been given by the people who had done that, and he tried to persuade him somehow to stay in his position, because, as he said, we were talking about a man who knew his job, who knew the unit, who knew how to use the unit, et cetera. Radovan would have none of that, and he told the commander: Sir, I'm no longer ready, I'm no longer able, because of the treatment I received on the hands of those paramilitary or para-something people. I can no longer put up with this, and I'm no longer prepared to put up with this, so I cannot stay in my position as commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Commander Nikolic's decision then?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this conversation, which didn't take too long, after trying to persuade him to stay in his position, Nikolic told Savic: You'll take over the command and you, Radovan, in view of your qualifications, will help out. The fringe areas of the line of defence will be your responsibility. It will be your responsibility to protect the people who are there. You'll build bunkers and shelters. And this was something he knew very well how to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. From that moment on, Radovan Antic, who had up to that point been the commander of the 4th Detachment, ceased to be the commander of the 4th Detachment, and you, Jovo Savic, were appointed the new commander of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me: Were there any other appointments, new appointments to the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Commander Nikolic told me the following: Savic, your deputy will be Captain First Class Milan Stojancevic. Simo Zaric was to stay in his position, and in order to avoid bringing completely new people in, we'll keep it this way for the time being. But should I see that there's need for further changes, you will be duly informed in a timely manner and you will receive an order in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other changes in the structure of the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was another change. I remember that Mr. Tadic then went to the civilian protection staff, to be their head, or commander, I'm not sure what the term was. I think it was the head of civilian protection. And he was replaced by Captain First Class, Mihajlo Topolovac [as interpreted], nicknamed Pile. He was well known by that nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us, roughly -- excuse me. My colleague is telling me something about the transcript. Mihajlo Topolovac or Mihajlo Tobirac?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihajlo Tobirac, called Pile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the command stay like that with those people working there? You as the commander, Stojancevic as your deputy, Zaric as assistant commander for security and Mihajlo Tobirac as assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command stayed like that until the beginning of June. That's I remained the commander for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about the event which occurred in Crkvina at the beginning of May, and how did you find out about it, about the crime committed by a man named Slobodan Miljkovic, also known as Lugar?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in the first half of May. Simo Zaric came to see us at the command. He was agitated. What people in our area usually refer to as beyond belief. It was beyond belief that a man's facial features could be so distorted, and also the way he speaks. And he said this, roughly: People, there's a problem that I can't face or accept as a human being, as a member of the unit. 16 people have been killed in Crkvina. That man over there, Lugar, he killed those people for no reason at all. When he told us this, believe me, we were shocked and angry. Was it possible for someone to commit a crime like that, we asked ourselves, against people whose only fault was that they were Croats and Muslims? Was it possible that -- this was a situation for us, as a consequence, where we were thinking about how to face this, how to oppose this, but we simply didn't know what to do. It was too much of a shock for us at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zaric do then when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric and Mr. Antic actually Mr. Zaric and Mr. Antic used their own channels to inform the Superior Command. They reported through their own channels the occurrence in Crkvina. They explained what sort of a crime that was. And Simo then told us that he would go immediately to Pelagicevo, that he would have to go. I believe he talked to his then superior, Makso Simeunovic, and then he was in touch with the commander. They said that Simo Zaric should immediately go to Pelagicevo, and then he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that Mr. Simo Zaric went to Belgrade on Commander Nikolic's orders?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know about that. Simo phoned from Pelagicevo, and he said that he had been given the task to go urgently to Belgrade on duty. It was a duty call. He phoned us and then after several days he was back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, was any decision made on the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska? Was any law passed? If you know anything about that, please tell us what you know about the law and when, roughly, it was passed.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first half of May, we heard that a law on the army of Republika Srpska was in the pipeline and that people from Yugoslavia, commanders from the area, would have to go to Serbia, or rather, Yugoslavia, and on the 12th of May, a law was adopted, the law on the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Mr. Antic [sic], you said a couple of answers ago that you knew that Mr. Zaric had been given the task to go urgently to Belgrade on duty. Do you know what that duty was, what mandate he was given, in terms of going to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simo Zaric called me from Pelagicevo, saying that he was ordered by the Tactical Group commander to immediately go to Belgrade on official duty. What his tasks were, you need to ask him, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So I understand from that answer that even though you were now his -- you were his -- one of his superiors in the 4th Detachment, you were not given any details, you did not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He wasn't obliged to inform me of the details. He just called to say that he was leaving because he was ordered to do so by the higher command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the Yugoslav People's Army withdraw its members from Bosnia and Herzegovina, from the territory of the Samac municipality, and if you know, tell us when did the members of the JNA leave the area of the Samac municipality or the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. After the 12th of May, there were extensive preparations for the departure of people, of the people from the JNA, senior officers. There weren't too many of them in our area. For example, at the Pelagicevo command, there were about four or five of them, six at the most. They were getting ready, and I know for sure that on the 19th of May, there were no officers or lower-ranking officers from the JNA at the Tactical Group any more. They had left for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the JNA did not only include officers, were there any soldiers of the JNA who were born in Serbia or Montenegro, who stayed on the territory of the Samac municipality, or was this only pertaining to the superior officers?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This referred only to the command staff. There were no soldiers from Yugoslavia there from Serbia. There were only command staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you can tell us: The soldiers of the 17th Tactical Group were mostly people who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e. who were born in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The command of the 17th Tactical Group, once they left, can we agree that the 17th Tactical Group ceased to exist any more and practically the 4th Detachment of the JNA also ceased to exist? What happened after that in the implementation of the law of the army of Republika Srpska? What were the units that were formed then in the area of the Samac and Pelagicevo municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army, we called that reformation. That's when the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade came into being, and the units of the brigade were subordinated. These were the former detachments, and they were now named battalions. This procedure took a while. It wasn't easy, if I can say, to reform a structure, to organise the records, to give people tasks according to their specialties, and also to organise the commanding and the soldier cadres. I would like to say that a number of people, until the formation of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, were not assigned according to their ability, to their specialty, to their profession, and so on, so this was one way of correcting this, for example, if somebody was in the artillery, they would be sent to a unit where there was an artillery section, engineers would be sent to an engineering unit. If somebody was in communications, and so on, they would be sent to the appropriate places. This took a certain amount of time. And then we had a new situation. We had battalions. We had lower-ranking units, and of course the highest command was the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, based in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, was there also a change in the area of responsibility? Was the 2nd Infantry Brigade much larger numbers-wise than the 17th Tactical Group? What happened with the 4th Detachment? Was that the same 4th Detachment which existed up until that time? Were there any differences there in the area of responsibility, in the numbers of personnel, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- or I know that the 2nd Posavina Brigade numbered for a while about 5.600 people, but I'm not sure about the numerical strength, when it was the Tactical Group. So I don't know whether there were more people there or fewer people there, in this unit or -- as compared to the previous unit. As far as the 4th Detachment is concerned, it was reformed into the 5th Battalion, just like the other battalions form detachments, they were all given specific numbers. So it was known exactly which was the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th, the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion's area of responsibility was expanded. One unit from Tisina came under my command, under the command of the 5th Battalion, and thereby their area of defence or area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of my battalion, was expanded by some ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, the numerical strength of the battalion was different.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion no longer included, as it did in the 4th Detachment, just citizens of the Samac municipality and town?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were some changes. The command staff, as well as the soldiers. The situation with them was changed. At the time, the 5th Battalion numbered about 510 people. I'm not exactly sure about that. This was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. So the command of the 5th Battalion was in fact the command which was also the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with some staff changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Zaric remain assistant commander for security and intelligence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric continued to perform his duties. He was functionally the assistant commander for intelligence and security, as well as for morale, and he continued to perform those duties in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please tell us: Who was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, because of the reformation of the units and the command, and so on, had some difficulties as a result of that. I know that in the beginning, an acquaintance of mine, Major Savic also, but his first name is Alijovika, he was there for a very short period of time, perhaps one day. And he left. He was a member of the Yugoslav army. And he originates from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but he left the command. I don't know what he was doing there. Then there was a kind of vacuum, and for a while nobody was commander. We, the commanders, only knew about this situation, and we did not wish to pass this information on to the rest of the army, amongst the soldiers, because of morale and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And then who was appointed commander?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihajlo Djurdjevic was appointed commander. He's from our area, from the village of Tisina, the Samac municipality. He was an experienced commanding officer, an experienced officer, with good organising abilities, a man of quality. People respected him and appreciated him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: What was the Superior Command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade? What was its name? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Posavina Brigade was resubordinated. Its Superior Command was the East Bosnia Corps, which was located in Bijeljina. That's what it was called at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So who could appoint the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the brigade is proposed by the corps command and appointed by the General Staff. Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did Colonel Djurdjevic, the commander, take up his duties as commander in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as he appeared, and this was -- I don't know exactly what date. Perhaps the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When he took up his duties as commander of the brigade, what was the first thing that Commander Colonel Djurdjevic did?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we heard this happy news that a man has come with experience. I've already said that. He called us all together, one day, the second or the third day after he arrived. He called all the commanders together and assistant commanders of the battalions for intelligence and security. We went to the command of the brigade to attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were there at that meeting, as the commander of the 5th Battalion, and Mr. Zaric as assistant commander for security and intelligence. Who else attended this meeting in Pelagicevo which was scheduled and conducted by brigade commander Colonel Djurdjevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides us, the battalion commanders, and our assistant commanders for security, the meeting was also attended by these people, guests, as he introduced them. There was Mr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, and there were also these representatives. I knew one of them. Representatives of the Orasje municipality. No, excuse me. Pelagicevo under formation. Milan Tanasic and another man was there with him, whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Stevan Todorovic. Who were they representing at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the commander say to you on that occasion, all of you who were present at that meeting? I mean Commander Djurdjevic.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Djurdjevic first of all greeted us. He welcomed his guests. Before that, of course, he introduced himself, because some people perhaps didn't know him. This was usual. Then he told us that he was the commander there now, and even though he's new in this area, that he is well-acquainted with the situation, aware of the problems and the situation with the troops, that he knows the problems and the situation in the entire zone of responsibility, knows that reformation was taking place, that was still under way, also that he was very strict in relation to people who were not militarily organised. He underlined the problem with the paramilitaries, with people who were police officers one day, were soldiers another day, and then the next day after that they even didn't know what they were, and so on. He literally said the following: Stevan Todorovic, you will either command that group of yours or allow me to command them. If neither of these things is done in this way, then I don't need them at all. The commander then said that we should not relax discipline. We must be very strict as soldiers, and disciplined, and we must do our job, because he will not tolerate any wilful behaviour. And I remember that he asked the representatives of the Pelagicevo municipality under formation, and the people from Samac, for logistical support, so that the army would be supplied in terms of receiving good food, and I know that Mr. Blagoje earlier had taken steps. He or some associate of his, for the same uniforms to be made up for the whole of the brigade. And I know that we often mention Mr. Blagoje in this context, that he was helping people, helping the units, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On this occasion, did he also set the condition that civilian authorities should not interfere in the activities or the work of the military?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was very explicit in this. There can be no interference in the command, with the command, or with the military. The civilian authority could only assist, upon his requests, but should not interfere in the command. The military has nothing to do with politics, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army, members of the army, what was their reaction to Commander Djurdjevic's, Colonel Djurdjevic's speech? And did the representatives of the civilian bodies of government too, in their own way, back Commander Djurdjevic in his intentions?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the meeting, the commanders and the assistants for security welcomed this with a great deal of relief. A burden fell off our backs. It was then I understood that we would turn into a proper army and that now was the right time to give it a shot. People from Samac and Pelagicevo, from the civilian structures who were present there were conspicuously satisfied. It was an interest we shared. The civilian structures on the one hand and the army, the military structures, on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please: What happened several days later, after the meeting in Pelagicevo had been held?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be very specific about the date, but I think about six or seven days later, not after the meeting, but rather after Mico had been appointed. We call him Mico, the colonel. I received a phone call. He phoned me and he told me to wait for him at the command, me and Simo should wait for him. He said: I'll come to see you. He asked: Where is Simo [Realtime transcript read in error "seemy"]? And I said: He has a day off today. He's not here. He said: Get hold of him and wait for me, both of you, at your own command. I waited for about two hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one clarification in the transcript, on page 15, line 15. Here it said "seemy." It's actually Simo. He was referring to the defendant Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could it also be corrected as to who "we" is. The transcript says we call Mico the colonel. Who is the we who will called Mico the colonel. I'm sorry, Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were about to clarify that. I have noticed this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when you speak, don't use names like Mico, Simo, please state these person's full names. Mico, the colonel, who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihajlo, also known as Mico. Both in town and village, this was an endearing term we used to refer to him. It was a slip, it won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mihajlo, called Mico.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the colonel who was the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think this will be set right. Told you and Simo. Which Simo? Was that Simo Zaric you were talking about? You and Simo Zaric [Realtime transcript read in error "Simo tzar"] waiting for the commander at the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to get this right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. This isn't really a mistake but --

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Simo, Simo, Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo, yes, Simo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to apologise. You were waiting for the commander. So what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he would be there within two hours, but he didn't show up. And then he phoned again and told me, Savic, because my name is Jovo Savic: Do you know where the Crisis Staff is? I knew where they were, because they were in the immediate vicinity. He said: Go there. You and Simo Zaric and wait for me there. I will be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just for clarity in the transcript. On page 16, line 13. I don't think we really want Mr. Simo Zaric referred to as a tzar. It says Simo tzar. Former Russian royal family and I think we should for the sake of clarity not have anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name was wrongly reflected in the transcript. It stated that Simo was a tzar. We were actually talking about Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking about Simo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were we talking about Simo Zaric or not? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were talking about Simo Zaric. I call him Zare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said he knew where the Crisis Staff was based, where its headquarters was, because it was in your immediate vicinity. Please tell us where exactly the Crisis Staff was and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Crisis Staff was at the heating plant. It used to be the town's heating plant. It was a facility like that. So those were the premises they were using at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simo Zaric did not go with you at that time, did he?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Simo only showed up a little later, so I went on my own. I met some people there, people I didn't know, but I did know a number of people there, Cedo Milicevic, an acquaintance of mine. We come from the same town. We had a cup of coffee together in his office waiting for the colonel and for Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please just repeat the name of the gentleman with whom you had coffee.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedo Milicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you set out to go to the heating plant, did you leave a message behind for Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told my duty officer and the duty communications officer that should Simo Zaric call or show up, they should tell him to immediately go to the Crisis Staff, because Colonel Mihajlo Djurdjevic would be waiting for him there, and I would be waiting for him there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. This place where you had coffee, was that a restaurant? Was that an office? Where was this office? Can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office was on the first floor. It was a small room. It was more like a kitchenette. It was next to the meeting or conference hall. It was in the same floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that room, you went straight into the conference room?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there's the corridor, and then off the corridor there's a door leading to the conference room, on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, did Commander Djurdjevic arrive?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he showed up. I saw him coming from the room, because the door was open. I stood up. I gave him a military salute. We've known each before, we come from the same area. He asked me how I was doing, all the pleasantries, and he said, let's go. I knocked on the door, we went into the conference room. President Blagoje was there, Mr. Stiv was there. There were chairs, so we sat down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjevic, the commander, was on his own. He was not accompanied by anyone when you met?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any other persons who were in that room which you and Commander Colonel Djurdjevic entered?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't many people there in the room. Savo Popovic was there, Aco Jankovic. I said already about Mr. Blagoje and Mr. Stiv. Another two or three persons I didn't know where there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any armed people in the room? What about the people you didn't know? Were they carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Aco Jankovic was carrying a handgun, but I'm not sure. I can't be sure. I did see armed people in front of the door outside the building, people I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps observe whether they were members of the so-called Sareni unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know many of those people over there, so I was sure that they were indeed from that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did the meeting go?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting took off in the following way: Mr. Blagoje welcomed us. The atmosphere was quiet and peaceful. We had a cup of coffee. We had some chitchat before the meeting began, and then the meeting began, the official part of the meeting, I should say. I can't recall all the details, but I'll try to think back as hard as I can. President Blagoje simply welcomed us. He acted as a true host. He offered a brief introduction and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brief introduction. What exactly did Mr. Blagoje say in those few brief introductory words?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: All right, soldiers. How are you doing? Mr. Colonel, we have had word that the army was not happy with you, that people were not happy, that they were complaining. We expected more and better from you. It was all along those lines, and this went on for about ten minutes. Then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hold on, please. You used the expression "people." Did he say "people" or "soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said "soldiers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stiv then took the floor and, in his usual way, voiced his dissatisfaction. He didn't want to talk about any colonel or about any senior officer who was prepared to do military work. But he said: We have a different solution. We'll go about this in a different way. He said I was in several units where the army was protesting, complaining. This old man, what good is he to us? He's well over the hill, and we need new, fresh forces. We need new people. He talked along these lines. And Simo Zaric showed up in the meantime. He sat down next to me, and Simo started speaking too, and Stiv was still talking, but Simo sort of gave me the secret nudge, as we say. And then I winked back at him. At one moment, Mr. Djurdjevic, in a very cool manner, in a slow and measured voice, like a true commander, addressed Mr. Blagoje, and he said that he, Stiv, Blagoje, and Colonel Djurdjevic, should stay together in the office and that the others should disperse. President Blagoje accepted that. He went along and he said: All right, gentlemen. This part of the meeting is over. Please. And then Colonel Mihajlo Djurdjevic turned to me and told me: Savic, you and Simo Zaric, wait for me downstairs. And that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you notice that after a while Blagoje Simic, Djurdjevic, and Stevan Todorovic were joined by Josko [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric and I were walking down those corridors. We'd pop by in an office to see our old acquaintance, Cedo Milicevic. And at one point, Dragan Djordjevic, also known as Crni, appeared, and he went to the conference room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He went to the room where the meeting was taking place?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe after about half an hour, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, also known as Stiv, came out. I could tell his voice among a thousand voices. There was a bit of chitchat, and he looked at me and he said: My congratulations. You have a new commander, Dragan Djordjevic, Crni. I said: Thank you. And he didn't say goodbye to Simo. And then Simo and I went back to our own command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you react to Stevan Todorovic congratulating you?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reaction. I didn't have a chance to tell him what I wanted to tell him, and that was: Stevan, my friend, this is no good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Did Commander Djurdjevic come out too?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, straight away. He took me by the hand and he said: Jovo Savic, you and Simo go to - Simo Zaric - go back to the units, keep working, keep the army together, watch over the army. Do your job, your regular job. I have been dismissed, but don't worry. Better times will come. Those were his exact words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and Zaric went back to your own command. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just one small correction. I believe that it was not an accurate translation of what the witness said, because here on page 22, line 3, it was translated here that the witness said, "Stevan, my friend, this is no good," which could suggest that the witness was friend with Stevan Todorovic, and this is not actually what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In fact, the meaning of this sentence from the witness is that the witness actually never said these words at all. Because he said he didn't have a chance to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and Stevan Todorovic friends before the war, during the war? What relationship did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic, called Stiv, as a high school student, was my tenant. He lived at my place, in my house, as a tenant, so I know him from those days. We were acquaintances. But we didn't socialise. We would just greet each other, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So who was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska after Commander Colonel Djurdjevic was replaced?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Djordjevic, called Crni, became the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. I didn't know that he was also given the rank of lieutenant colonel. So there was some correspondence in which -- and some documents in which he signed himself as Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Djordjevic. And that's him, and I know also that his nickname is Crni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he really have that rank or was he given that rank when he was appointed as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained already how ranks are awarded in the army. This is a procedure that takes some time for a person to be a lieutenant colonel, and I know this very well. He needs to spend a certain amount of time in a lower rank. He needs to be a major, then a lieutenant colonel. In order to do that, he needs to be in that duty for at least four years, with a very positive grade or assessment from his superior officer. So I don't know how Lieutenant Colonel Djordjevic, called Crni, received this rank. In my opinion, this was not legal. I didn't know that he was really a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have information about who appointed him commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information was that someone, some superior officer, Dencic, or something like that - I don't know - did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was appointed chief of the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of the brigade was another man, a volunteer from Serbia, called Debeli. His name was Srecko Radovanovic, called Debeli.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, also a volunteer from Serbia? Do you know who was the commander of the military police unit in the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. The military police unit was commanded by a man that I didn't know. He was a volunteer. Zlatan -- I don't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to help you and tell you that, according to our information, his name was Zvjezdan, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zvjezdan. Yes, that's right. Nobody knew any other name, just Zvjezdan. We didn't know his last name. When I would see that man, he was quite a hefty person, bulky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. With the new command in the 2nd Posavina Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, your question wasn't answered. You asked the witness whether Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was also a volunteer from Serbia. There is no answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he did answer that question. Perhaps this was not recorded down in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, also a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, yes. This wasn't recorded, so it needs to be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Before you just move on to this part of your questioning. I wonder whether, Mr. Antic [sic], as a military man yourself, you have some knowledge how Commander Djurdjevic could be dismissed at this meeting in the conference room where the people who were present were Dr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Stevan Todorovic. Where was their authority to dismiss him because you've said earlier that the civilian authorities didn't interfere with the military, and vice versa. So I'm just wondering how, in this meeting, in this conference room, which later the new lieutenant colonel, otherwise known as Crni, went into, could have produced this result. And I think the Trial Chamber would be interested in hearing a little bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understood Her Honour Judge Williams's question. Just one thing. This has happened another time. Mr. Savic has for the second time been addressed as Mr. Antic. I think these are slight problems with our last names. But this witness's name is Jovo Savic, and this is just for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Savic. Not that I muddled you up. Slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour. I will tell you that I don't know who was at that point authorised to replace Colonel Djurdjevic and to appoint Dragan Djordjevic, called Crni, to that post. I don't know who was authorised to do that, and I don't know who it was that replaced him. I know that he was at the meeting and that after that, Djordjevic, Dragan, called Crni, was appointed commander. I don't know. I don't know who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were the -- we said that you were the commander of the 5th Battalion, so that practically the commander of the 2nd Infantry Brigade, Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was your superior officer.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after that, to you as the commander of the 4th -- no, I mean the 5th Battalion of the army of Republika Srpska? Could you please tell the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I cannot remember the dates all that well - many years have passed since then - sometime in early June I was carrying out my every day regular duties. Stevan Todorovic, called Stiv, called me on the telephone, asked me what I was doing and where is Roda. And I will explain who Roda is. Roda is a younger man, Mladen Radovic, aka Roda, he was my driver. When he asked me: Where is Roda, I answered well, yes, he's here, close by. Stevan Todorovic then said: Why don't you come to my -- to where I am right away. He was at the department store at the time. That's where his office was. It was the Posavka department store in Bosanski Samac. Your commander is waiting for you here. Of course, my driver turned the engine on in the vehicle. We got into the car and we went to the department store and went upstairs to the chief of the public security station, Stevan Todorovic's office. The commander was present there, Djordjevic. I greeted him. We sat down. We probably had something to drink, coffee, juice, or a drink. And Dragan Djordjevic asked me what was this man, Roda, doing? And he referred to him as "my Roda." I said that he was a good driver, a quiet man, drove and maintained the vehicle. He was steady, reliable, and so on. Then Lieutenant Djordjevic, called Crni, my commander, addressed my driver, called Roda, and said: Would you like to be a commander man? And I was at a loss. I was surprised. I thought that he was joking. I could tell by the driver that he -- he shrugged his shoulders, as we say, as if he were accepting that. And that was the end of the story. Then Crni, Lieutenant Colonel Djordjevic, said: Roda, you and me are going to the Pelagicevo command, and you, Savic, go to the unit. I must say also that this man, Lieutenant Colonel Djordjevic, when he talks, he talks very quickly. Sometimes it's difficult to understand him. It's unintelligible. So the way I understood it was that I was being replaced from my post and that I was being replaced by my driver, called Roda. I went to my command. There were two company commanders there, Vlado Sisic and another one, I think his name was Dzemal. Maybe it wasn't him. Maybe it was someone else, but it doesn't matter. We sat down, and one of the commanders asked me this, Vlado Sisic. He said: Commander, you seem to be in a bad mood. I tried to pretend as if nothing had happened, and so on, but it didn't really work. Then I called together the company commanders and told them, and I told them not to worry too much. I was still going to stay there. But I would be just a general affairs officer or a clerk, and I would be managing the general affairs and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were replaced, and you went to the post of general affairs clerk?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who became the commander of the 5th Battalion of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 5th Battalion, the battalion that I headed up until then, became, on that same day, Mladen Radovic, called Roda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since Radovic Mladen was under your command, you probably know whether he had any rank of a reserve military officer or did he have any military education or training or anything like that? Tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any rank, either of an officer or a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was just a regular soldier. Thank you. So how long did you stay in the 5th Battalion of the army of Republika Srpska carrying out these general duties in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the 5th Battalion until the 1st of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit were you transferred to on the 1st of September, 1992, and what changes took place, generally, in the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the order that I was being transferred to the command of the brigade, of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, to carry out duties of clerk in the training and operative -- operations department, and that I should report for duty on the 5th of September. When I came to the brigade command and reported there, in accordance with this order, I was seen by captain -- First Class Captain Jondic, Vojin, who introduced me to the major, Mile Beronja, who became the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. So he introduced me to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the commander of Captain Beronja?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile Beronja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened with the hitherto commander, Dragan Djordjevic, Crni? How was he replaced? How was it that a new commander was appointed in the person of Captain Mile Beronja?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this happened, but I know that Crni and the group that was around him went away. They were arrested. I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we have the following situation. There is a new command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. Can you tell us, if you know, when Mr. Simo Zaric came to that brigade and what post in the command of the brigade was he occupying?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Simo Zaric came together with me on the 5th of September, and I know for sure that Simo Zaric was appointed assistant commander for morale and legal affairs in the brigade command, morale, information, and legal affairs. That is the name of his post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I remember well, that body was called the department for morale, legal, and religious affairs. If my memory serves me right. Could you please tell us what that body was called.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, yes. I really apologise. The body or the department, headed by Simo Zaric, as assistant commander, was called the department for morale, religious, and legal affairs. The information part was actually something that applied to the battalion. So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. This may be just a question of translation, but I'm wondering why an assistant commander in a military infantry brigade would be in charge of religious affairs. I wonder whether you could just briefly say what you know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer the question by Judge Williams.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll tell you. In addition to working with morale, religious affairs implied the following: Whenever there were burials, and unfortunately there were quite many, religious ceremonies, the last rites, the speeches, all of this was part of the job description. Simo Zaric was not a priest. He was merely an administrator linking up all these different areas of activity related to a person's burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please: The command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, how many members did it have? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the brigade command, we were 13 members all together. We had a commander, chief of staff, personnel, operations section, security, morale, and logistics. These were the different subsections that made up the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, please: From which military unit did Commander Major Mile Beronja come? I want to know about the corps. I'm not really interested in the official unit.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came from the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what its name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade command, at its meetings, did they discuss the state of morale of brigade members? Did they discuss the reasons for such a situation? Did it take any decisions as to what to do in that respect?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the bodies, or rather, subsections that I've mentioned earlier had the duty, very often in writing, to right the situation in their own area, that is the situation in the unit, not in the command, throughout the units. Among other things, Simo Zaric, as assistant commander for morale, was duty-bound to send an official report once a month to the corps command, the then East Bosnian Corps. In order for this monthly report to be written, you need several days. You visit the subordinated units, you visit the soldiers on the front lines, you try to get an insight into what people are doing, how they feel, the way they think, and a number of other activities too. Sometimes, and even more frequently than that, not only Simo Zaric, but other people from the command, once they're ordered to, would go and visit the units, would visit defence lines and talk to people, depending on the area and who was controlling the unit, in order to get an idea of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late September, at the brigade command meeting of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, was there a conclusion to draw up a report concerning morale and the reasons for this situation? Who from the command was in charge of preparing, of drafting this more comprehensive report on morale?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he came back from visiting the unit, Simo Zaric had the duty to inform the commander, and there were daily meetings of the different command bodies, sometimes in the morning, sometimes in the evening. And people would come from the different ethnic groups and they would report. Simo Zaric got the task from Commander Major Mile Beronja to write a report for our internal use. Some sections of this report he was told to forward, or rather, the whole report, to the East Bosnian Corps. I think there was a colonel and I think his name was Dosen, but really, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did the command discuss this information as contained in the report written by Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. On several occasions when this report was being drafted, we had briefings, and one of us members would make amendments or additions to the report. We tried to be helpful. Simo was in charge. That was his job. I can even say that 90 per cent of the information contained therein was information that he had obtained. It was, after all, his duty. At brigade command level, this report was debated for a long time, and eventually, at the end of November, I think perhaps on the 27th, but I don't have a very good head for dates --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We unanimously adopted this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take your time, please. The brigade command considered this report, reviewed this report. Was everyone in attendance, all the members of the command?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everyone, all the members of the command were in attendance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any representatives from the East Bosnian Corps present at that meeting when this report was adopted?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two colonels were there. I may go wrong there. I'm not sure about their last names, but again, I think it was Dosen and Jakovljevic. I may be wrong there, but I believe it was the two of them, from the East Bosnian Corps, at that particular meeting where we adopted the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had this debate, and this report. How was it adopted? The way documents are usually adopted? Was there voting? Was it a unanimous decision?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one voted against this report. It was a unanimous decision. As soon as you signed, I know that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it then that all members of the command decided to sign the report?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Members of the command, did they all sign it at the same time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same day, at the same meeting, when it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign it too?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this might be a convenient time to break, because I would like the report to be shown to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. May the witness please be shown Exhibit Number P127.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic, can you please have a look at this document, familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this document. This is the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was being written and when it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the document, the report, which you adopted at the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now please look at the last page of this document. Do you see the signatures there? Tell me, please, and read out whose name is under number 7 of this list. Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7, Captain First Class, Jovo Savic, administrator for operations and training, and that is me. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the signatures of other members of the command that we can see here are indeed their signatures?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This certainly looks identical to their signatures. I know most of their signatures, and of course I know the people. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not wish to discuss this document, but we have ascertained that this is indeed the document. And under number 7 we see your signature.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will not be needing this document now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade adopted this report? Was there a meeting? When? How? Who was present? Please tell us, if you know.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, Commander Mile Beronja told us that we would have a meeting on that day and that we would have visitors. The meeting was held in a room. We used to call it the restaurant. In addition to the members of the command, other persons were present, persons from Samac, Mr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, Mr. Milan Simic, maybe some other persons too, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, did Stevan Todorovic, also known as Stiv, attend that meeting too?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I forgot about him. And there was another person too. Stevan Todorovic was there, and another man who said he was from the SUP, or from the MUP. He was some sort of chief or head. I think his name was Minic, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person from MUP, what is the MUP? That's the Ministry of the Interior; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was discussed at that meeting? What happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting, the report was discussed, the report written by the command, or rather, members of the command who wrote it. A certain amount of discontent was voiced by a number of people, especially those who were visitors, and then I remember that Stevan Todorovic was the most vociferous one. He was saying: What are you really after? Who do you think you are? This just isn't right. You want to get people to quarrel. You want to get people to clash with the army. And so on and so forth. It was a very heated debate. At one point, this person from the SUP, from the Ministry of the Interior, threatened the members of the command. He said that there would be acts of repression, that there would be criminal reports against people, that people would be punished. It was all about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took part in this discussion on behalf of the command? Could all members of the command take the floor? Specifically, I want to know if Commander Beronja then allowed Mr. Simo Zaric to take part in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Simo Zaric wanted to speak, but Commander Mile Beronja said: No. Sit down. Simo didn't say a word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was the meeting concluded?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a rather unusual way, I'll say. There was almost a punch-up. A member of ours, a member of the command who was one of the signatories of the report, his name was Jovan Erletic. At one point he sprang to his feet and faced Minic, saying, from the Ministry of the Interior, he said: Who are you to be telling us all this? Who do you want? And then they almost started fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me get this right. At this meeting, there were no conclusions that were adopted from both sides?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened later with Mr. Zaric, and what happened to him later, as a member of the command in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, Simo Zaric was returned to one of the units as a regular soldier. He was degraded, as we say. He was assistant commander and then he became just a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After how long did you say? After how much time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps a couple of days passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I would like to go back now to an event that exposed you and Mr. Zaric to certain contacts with the members of these volunteers. Do you remember the situation when the corridor in the village of Kornica was closed, or the village of Gornja Slatina? Who closed it, and what did you and Mr. Zaric experience when you were going to your work at the command in Pelagicevo, to the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander, Beronja, sent us to Samac. I remember it was autumn. It was a little bit misty or foggy. And we were going in the direction of Samac. At one checkpoint of the civilian police in Crkvina, we were stopped by a policeman, an acquaintance of ours. Both Simo and I knew him. His name was Djordje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to give us the name.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he said the following to us: The two of you, be careful. Lugar and his team are looking for you. And this was something that would send shivers down to your bones, to be in such a situation. Simo and I continued on our way to Samac. We drove quickly, and we were thinking in the car, and just talking about what to do and where to go. He suggested that we go to his apartment, and I suggested that we go to my house. Still, we decided to go to his apartment, but in front of the building where he lives, we saw a Golf vehicle. One man in this vehicle with a hood on his head. We thought that this was somebody who was waiting for us, so very quickly we turned into a small street, put the car in the garage, and as fast as we were able to, we went into his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "Lugar and his team"? What did you mean by that? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar had this group of people around him who were similar to him. These were volunteers. We call them Sareni, specials. This is what they call themselves. That is who I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, when, in which month, if you can remember the approximate dates? When was this corridor closed? When did this take place?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was in November. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Lugar came to be in this area, Lugar and this group of his? Under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under Stiv's command. I thought that they had already left, gone somewhere, because I wouldn't see them in Pelagicevo. Perhaps some of them would stop by at Pelagicevo. But we didn't really have any contacts. They were under Stiv's command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did this policeman tell you so that you and Mr. Zaric got so worried and were getting ready to hide and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Lugar is a man who, as we say, will stop at nothing. He doesn't care. He can beat a man, kick him, impose his will on him. In other words, this was a man who had something happening in his head. Sometimes it seemed to me as if he had gone mad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, did this police officer tell you something to make you so worried about your lives? I mean, you said you had gone to hide.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as he mentioned the words "Lugar and his team," that was enough to mean run and hide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid for your lives?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were afraid down to our very bones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo and I spent the whole night taking turns, keeping watch. One slept for a while, while the other was awake. After this person that we saw in the Golf, the man in the hood, sometime after midnight, this vehicle went away, and we got up -- now it was quite foggy, and we were thinking what to do now. We didn't have any communications with our Superior Command so that we could inform them of the situation that we were in. We decided to take the same road back. When we approached Kornica, immediately in the vicinity of this checkpoint, we realised that we had made a mistake in going back, because we had picked up somebody on the way, a man, a civilian. And we were stopped by one of the police officers. Lugar approached us and said: You can see the birds are now in a package. This is what he said to us. And the package was actually Simo and myself. He didn't know this third man. He asked us: Where are you going, gentlemen? Simo Zaric replied: To work. And he continued with his question: What work? What kind of work? What kind of a brigade is this? There were all of these additional questions. And then from the right side, a member approached. I was his uncle, and he happened to be in this team. He said: Uncle, what are you doing here? And probably when Lugar heard this exchange of ours, he said the following: You can go to that sorry command of yours. I will come to see you. I don't want to see any one of you run. Simo and I went to our workplace. We knew where Colonel Novica Simic was. I'm not sure whether he was a general at that point. Anyway, we dropped by to see him and briefly explained to Mr. Novica Simic what was happening at Kornica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Novica Simic, what was his duty at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander of the East Bosnia Corps, but at the time, he happened to be in Donji Zabar, in a facility called Agroposavina. That was his forward command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say once you had informed him of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the following: Men, you go back to your unit command. I'm sick and tired of them as well. I'm thinking of the volunteers. I have already taken certain steps to get rid of that gang. I have started the armoured battalion moving. I have prepared the artillery in order to cover them. Then I said: Colonel, sir, very close to that checkpoint where we were stopped is the house of my wife's parents and my two children. And the colonel said the following thing: Savic, get your wife and children out of there, in any way that you can, and tell your family to leave that place. We went to our command and we informed our commander, Beronja, about what was happening, and he said: You two have to be careful. Watch out for those fools, and they're really not a good lot. You have to watch yourself. And this is how the whole story ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You use this term "to cover them by artillery." Could you please clearly explain for the transcript and for the Trial Chamber exactly what you mean by that term.

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will explain. This is a slang term. To cover by artillery means to actually cover a certain area by artillery fire, a certain area that is covered by that fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the commander, Simic, was planning to hit that checkpoint by artillery fire, the checkpoint that was closing the corridor, and open fire at all the people who happened to be at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is probably what he meant to do, I mean, if he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in a situation to attend, as part of an official delegation of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, any municipal ceremonies or fetes, and if so, did you have any meetings with anyone, and if you did, what were these contacts? What was the content of such contacts? What happened during these occasions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, when we were celebrating our army holidays, it was in our practice always to have people from the Samac municipality attend. They would also invite us back, also to their celebrations. I remember on one occasion, two or three of us were invited to, I think -- no, I don't think, I know that Beronja, Major Beronja was there, the Chief of Staff, Milan Josic was there. He was a captain. And myself. We went to this hotel for the celebration of the -- to mark the town holiday. I don't remember exactly what the occasion was. But this lunch was not as pleasant as we expected it to be. It was spoiled for us by Stiv, who tried to tell us that we were not welcome, that we were Commis, that the 4th Detachment was an Ustasha detachment. What are you thinking? I think that he was in a semi-intoxicated state, but regardless of that, I know him well, since he was a young man, so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say that you were Commis?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that we were Commis, that we were no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know the date that was celebrated as the day of the Samac municipality, its holiday? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have a couple more questions. You are an officer. Could you please tell us when a soldier can refuse to implement an order issued by his superior? In which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier can refuse to implement an order from his superior only in case -- in the event that such an order would border on or constitute a criminal act or would result in some adverse consequences for people or materiel equipment, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've received information from you so far that the 4th Detachment received three orders from the commander of the 17th Tactical Group in the course of the 17th of April, 1992. This is the order on the detachment's mobilisation. In your opinion, does this order constitute a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second order, to take up defensive lines on the Bosanski Samac embankment, is that something that would constitute a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: JOVO SAVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I appreciate the answer was given before I could jump in and object, but the witness has just given two answers which he's been asked to express a legal opinion. It's one thing for the witness to give a view and his experience as an officer. It's quite another for him to express an opinion for which he has not been qualified before this Tribunal to do so. So I object to answers as to whether things were legal or not, as opposed to what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence cannot agree with this approach or this standpoint of the Prosecution. If a soldier is asked to differentiate between a criminal act, what runs against certain interests, or has the choice not to commit a criminal act, each man, each soldier, has enough civic education in order to be able to differentiate between orders that constitute a criminal act and the ones that do not. They don't have to be legal experts. This is prescribed under the law and is contained in international conventions. How could he refuse to do something if he's not aware that something constitutes a criminal act?
